title: Organisation policies: guardrails inherited down the tree

videos.script: IAM says who may do something. An organisation policy says what may be done at all, by anybody. {{two}} Even an owner cannot create a key in a project where keys are forbidden. That is what makes it a guardrail. {{owner}} A constraint is a rule Google defines. A policy is that rule, set to a value, on a node of the tree. {{constraint}} And the tree matters again. A policy on the organisation reaches every project. A folder lower down may keep it, merge with it, or replace it. {{tree}} Merging is where people get it wrong. For a list of places that are allowed, merging adds places. So a folder meant to be stricter ends up looser. {{merge}} You will write three guardrails for planner. Two places to run, one place for production, and no keys. {{three}} The third goes in as a dry run first. It refuses nothing, and it writes down everything it would have refused. {{dryrun}} Then Terraform plans all three, and you read the one line that decides the estate. {{end}}
